name: HI-MAP (Hierarchical Imitation of Mixed Agent Policies)
analogy: Think of it as a trading desk manager who has learned, by watching, which of the desk's specialists to hand the book to at any moment: the mean-reversion trader in a quiet range, the breakout trader on a big morning, the closer who flattens everything before the session ends.

steps.title: Build a library of specialist policies
steps.description: Gather several sub-policies that each trade well in a narrow situation. They can come from rules, from past human decisions or from earlier trained models. None of them has to be good everywhere.
steps.inExample: Three specialists are collected: a mean-reversion policy, a breakout policy and a flatten-before-the-close policy, all acting on 5-minute MNQ bars.

steps.title: Record which specialist was in charge for each bar
steps.description: For each historical bar, the demonstrations say which specialist a skilled trader or a rule set was using, and what action it took. The specialist labels, not the raw trades, are what the top level learns from.
steps.inExample: At 10:05 the demonstrations mark the breakout policy; at 12:30 they mark mean reversion; at 15:50 they mark the flatten policy.

steps.title: Teach the selector to imitate the choice
steps.description: The high-level selector reads the bar's features and learns to predict which specialist the demonstrations would pick. It copies the assignment decision rather than any single trade.
steps.inExample: After training, given a wide opening bar with heavy volume, the selector leans strongly toward the breakout specialist.

steps.title: Teach each specialist its own behavior
steps.description: Each low-level policy is trained to copy the actions of its demonstrated expert in the situations where it is assigned. This warm start removes the slow trial-and-error search a fresh agent would need.
steps.inExample: The breakout policy learns to enter in the direction of a bar that closes beyond the prior 12-bar high, sized at 2 contracts.

steps.title: Fine-tune the whole stack with rewards
steps.description: Once the copies work, reinforcement learning with a profit-and-cost reward improves the selector and the specialists together. A penalty keeps the selector from drifting too far from what it copied, so it can improve on the demonstrations without inventing odd behavior.
steps.inExample: Trading costs of about 1 US dollar per contract per side are charged, which teaches the selector to avoid switching specialists on every bar.

steps.title: Blend or choose at decision time
steps.description: On a new bar the selector outputs a weight for each specialist. The system can follow the single top choice or mix the specialists' actions by those weights. A flat specialist can take over when the selector is unsure.
steps.inExample: At 10:35 the weights are 62 percent breakout, 30 percent mean reversion and 8 percent flatten, so the blended action is a small long position of 1 contract.

useFor.task: Blending a trend specialist and a range specialist
useFor.example: Letting one selector decide, bar by bar on MNQ 5-minute data, whether the breakout rules or the fade rules should be steering right now.
Learning from a logged history of which approach a trader used in each situation, then using rewards to improve on that history.
Allocating control among three finished strategies on ES and MNQ so that each one trades only in the regimes where it has worked.

useFor.task: Handling the open and the close separately
useFor.example: Giving the first 15 minutes after the cash open and the last 10 minutes before the close their own dedicated specialists.
Routing to a do-nothing specialist when the selector's confidence collapses around a scheduled economic release.

avoidWhen: You have no trustworthy specialists or demonstrations to imitate; a single model trained directly on labeled outcomes is simpler and does not inherit anyone's blind spots.
The specialists are all near-copies of one idea; the selector then has nothing real to choose between and only adds complexity.

example.scenario: At 10:35 Eastern on an MNQ session, the system has three specialists and must decide who controls the next 5-minute bar after a strong opening drive.

input.summary: The current bar's features plus the position the system already holds.

fields.name: close
fields.meaning: The price at which the 10:35 five-minute bar closed, rounded to a whole point.

fields.name: average true range, 14 bars
fields.meaning: The typical high-to-low travel of a recent bar, showing that the market is moving widely.

fields.name: close against prior 12-bar high
fields.meaning: How far the close sits beyond the highest price of the previous twelve bars.

fields.name: volume against its 20-bar average
fields.meaning: How heavy trading in this bar was compared with the recent norm; here a little over double.

fields.name: minutes since the cash open
fields.meaning: How far into the trading session the bar sits, which separates open, midday and close behavior.

fields.name: current position
fields.meaning: The system holds no contracts going into this bar.

output.summary: A weight for each specialist and the action those weights produce.

fields.name: weight on breakout specialist
fields.meaning: How much control the selector gives the breakout policy for this bar.

fields.name: weight on mean-reversion specialist
fields.meaning: How much control the selector gives the fade policy for this bar.

fields.name: weight on flatten specialist
fields.meaning: How much control the selector gives the stay-flat policy for this bar.

fields.name: blended action
fields.meaning: The position change produced by mixing the three specialists' actions with those weights.

example.reading: The selector is leaning on the breakout specialist but not fully, so the system takes a small position rather than a full one. Watch the weights across bars: weights that jump around from bar to bar mean the selector is unstable, and every switch costs commission and slippage.
